s: date-palm is propagated by shoots (from full-grown trees)
q: They are usually propagated from shoots of full grown trees, which if transplanted and taken care of, will yield in six or seven years, whilst those raised immediately from the stone require sixteen years to produce fruit.

s: date-palm produces dates (fifteen or twenty clusters annually at full vigour)
q: bearing anually fifteen or twenty clusters of dates, each of them fifteen or twenty pounds in weight;

s: date-palm requires water (at the roots once in four or five days)
q: The only culture requisite, is to be well watered at the roots once in four or five days, and to have the lower boughs cut off when they begin to droop and wither.

s: date-palm produces sap, or honey of the palm (delicious and wholesome when drunk quite fresh)
q: The sap, or honey of the palm is a delicious and wholesome beverage when drunk quite fresh;

s: Jereed is part of Sahara (Tunisian portion)
q: El-Jereed, or Belad-el-Jereed, the country of dates, or literally, the country of the palm branches, is a part of the Sahara, or the hot dry country lying in the immediate vicinity of the Great Desert.

s: date-palm is used for tapping the palm (when it produces little fruit)
q: When a tree is found not to produce much fruit, the head is cut off, and a bowl or cavity scooped out of the summit, in which the rising sap is collected

s: date-palm provides palm branches (for baskets and wickerwork)
q: The most beautiful baskets, and a hundred other nick-nackery of the wickery sort are made of its branches

s: date-palm provides palm fibres (for ropes and vestments)
q: ropes are made and vestments wove from the long fibres

s: date-palm provides palm wood (for building when hardened by age)
q: and its wood, also, when hardened by age, is used for building.

s: palm-groves is a a beautiful object
q: A palm-grove is really a beautiful object, and requires scarcely less attention than a vineyard.

s: irrigation improves date-palm (through frequent watering)
q: For this tree, which loves a warm climate, and a sandy soil, is yet wonderfully improved by frequent irrigation

s: irrigation uses small channels (from streams to individual trees)
q: The water is drawn by small channels from the stream to each individual tree, around the stalk and root of which a little basin is made and fenced round with clay

s: date cultivation requires irrigation (in spring and throughout summer)
q: Irrigation is performed in the spring, and through the whole summer.

s: Jereed is called Tunisian Sahara (properly called)
q: The Belad-el-Jereed, therefore, may be properly called the Tunisian Sahara.

s: date trade is based on dates (principal resource of El-Jereed)
q: The trade and resources of this country consist principally in dates.

s: Jereed was occupied by Romans (as shown by antiquities)
q: The Jereed, from the existence in it of a few antiquities, such as pieces of granite and marble, and occasionally a name or a classic inscription, is proved to have been in the possession of the Romans

s: Jereed was occupied by Carthaginians (before the Romans)
q: and undoubtedly of the Carthaginians before them

s: Tafilett is a date-country (in Morocco)
q: Besides the Jereed, Tafilett, in Morocco, is a great date-country.

s: Bey of the Camp is a heir-apparent (to the Tunisian throne)
q: who administers affairs in this country as a sovereign; and who, indeed, is heir-apparent to the Tunisian throne.

s: Bey of the Camp collects tribute (through an annual flying-camp)
q: The duties of the "Bey of the Camp" is to visit with a "flying-camp," for the purpose of collecting tribute, the two circuits or divisions of the Regency.

s: tribute collection is conducted by Bey of the Camp (through the flying-camp)
q: The duties of the "Bey of the Camp" is to visit with a "flying-camp," for the purpose of collecting tribute, the two circuits or divisions of the Regency.

s: the expedition and camp is used for tribute collection (by the Bey of the Camp)
q: The duties of the "Bey of the Camp" is to visit with a "flying-camp," for the purpose of collecting tribute

s: Tour to the Jereed describes Jereed (in succeeding pages)
q: I now introduce to the reader the narrative of a Tour to the Jereed, extracted from the notebooks of the tourists, together with various observations of my own interspersed, and some additional account of Toser, Nefta, and Ghafsa.

s: Jereed contains El-Sibhah (vast salt lake or salt plain)
q: Besides the grand natural feature of innumerable lofty and branching palms, whose dark depending slender leaves, are depicted by the Arabian poet as hanging gracefully like the dishevelled ringlets of a beautiful woman in distress, there is the vast salt lake, El-Sibhah, or literally the "salt plain," and called by some modern geographers the Sibhah-el-Soudeeat, or Lake of Marks, from having certain marks made of the trunks of the palm, to assist the caravans in their marches across its monotonous samelike surface.

s: El-Sibhah is a salt lake (also a salt plain)
q: there is the vast salt lake, El-Sibhah, or literally the "salt plain,"

s: El-Sibhah is called Sibhah-el-Soudeeat (by some modern geographers)
q: and called by some modern geographers the Sibhah-el-Soudeeat, or Lake of Marks

s: El-Sibhah extends seventy English miles (from north-east to south-west)
q: The lake measures from north-east to south-west about seventy English miles, with a third of the breadth

s: Captain B. is a tourist (of the tour to the Jereed)
q: The tourists were Captain Balfour, of the 88th Regiment, and Mr. Richard Reade, eldest son of Sir Thomas Reade.

s: the expedition and camp contains 2,660 people (including troops and Arab camp followers)
q: The force of the camp consisted of--Mamelukes of the Seraglio, superbly mounted 20 Mamelukes of the Skeefah, or those who guard the entrance of the Bey's palace, or tent, and are all Levantines 20 Boabs, another sort of guard of the Bey, who are always about the Bey's tent, and must be of this country 20 Turkish Infantry 300 Spahis, o. mounted Arab guards 300 Camp followers (Arabs) 2,000 ----- Total 2,660

s: the expedition and camp includes Turkish Infantry (300 men)
q: The force of the camp consisted of--Mamelukes of the Seraglio, superbly mounted 20 Mamelukes of the Skeefah, or those who guard the entrance of the Bey's palace, or tent, and are all Levantines 20 Boabs, another sort of guard of the Bey, who are always about the Bey's tent, and must be of this country 20 Turkish Infantry 300

s: the expedition and camp includes Arab camp followers (2,000 Arabs)
q: Spahis, o. mounted Arab guards 300 Camp followers (Arabs) 2,000 ----- Total 2,660

s: Turkish Infantry is a irregular infantry (Turkish troops in the expedition)
q: We noticed particularly the 300 Turkish infantry; they were irregulars with a vengeance, though regulars compared to the Arabs.

s: Turkish Infantry number 300 (in the force of the camp)
q: Turkish Infantry 300

s: Nithalm is absent from the Bey's expedition (the new corps was entirely absent)
q: We may notice the total absence of any of the new corps, the Nithalm.

s: the Bey's expedition includes two pieces of artillery
q: Besides the above-named troops, there were two pieces of artillery.

s: R. is a tourist (of the tour to the Jereed)
q: The tourists were Captain Balfour, of the 88th Regiment, and Mr. Richard Reade, eldest son of Sir Thomas Reade.

s: the Bey's expedition passes through the plain of Manouba (on the route from the Bardo)
q: The Bey proceeded across the plain of Manouba, mounted on a beautiful bay charger, in front of the colours, towards Beereen, the greater part of the troops of the expedition following

s: the march has speed about four miles per hour (average pace with horses, camels, and other animals walking)
q: Through the whole of the route we marched on an average of about four miles per hour, the horses, camels, &c., walking at a good pace.

s: the march uses the water supply (water is carried from Tunis by camels)
q: A man followed the Bey about holding in his hand a golden cup, and leading a mule, having two paniers on its back full of water, which was brought from Tunis by camels.

s: the water supply originates in Tunis (carried to camp by camels)
q: A man followed the Bey about holding in his hand a golden cup, and leading a mule, having two paniers on its back full of water, which was brought from Tunis by camels.

s: the bastinado is a punishment (generally formal and intended as terror)
q: In general, it may be said that bastinadoing in Tunis is a matter of form, many of the strokes ordered to be inflicted being never performed, and those given being so many taps or scratches.

s: the bastinado is inflicted on the culprit (his hands and feet tied behind him)
q: The bastinado was inflicted by two inferior mamelukes, standing one on each side of the culprit, who had his hands and his feet tied behind him.

s: Tunis has rarely severe punishments (severe punishments of any kind are uncommon)
q: Severe punishments of any kind are rarely inflicted in Tunis.

s: the hyaena is a wild animal (principally noted for stupidity when at large)
q: The hyaena is not the savage beast commonly represented; he rarely attacks any person, and becomes untameably ferocious by being only chained up. He is principally remarkable for his stupidity when at large in the woods.

s: the hyaena inhabits Atlas Mountains (abundant in its forests)
q: The animal abounds in the forests of the Morocco Atlas.

s: the lion inhabits Atlas Mountains (prefers thick brushwood and rocky ravines to sandy open plains)
q: Very thick brushwood, and ground broken with rocks, like the ravines of the Atlas, are his haunts.

s: R. is a eldest son of Sir Thomas Reade
q: The tourists were Captain Balfour, of the 88th Regiment, and Mr. Richard Reade, eldest son of Sir Thomas Reade.

s: gazelles is a swift animal (described as having the speed of a greyhound)
q: One of the last gave us a good chase, but the greyhounds caught him; in the first half mile, he certainly beat them by a good half of the instance, but having taken a turn which enabled the dogs to make a short cut, and being blown, they pulled the swift delicate creature savagely down.

s: Mr. Reade tour in Jereed
q: CHAPTER IX. Tour in the Jereed of Captain Balfour and Mr. Reade.

s: Sidi Mohammed is a Bey of the Camp
q: The morning before starting from Tunis they went to the Bardo to pay their respects to Sidi Mohammed, "Bey of the Camp," and to thank him for his condescending kindness in taking them with him to the Jereed.

s: Sidi Mohammed left the Bardo (at nine A. M.)
q: At nine A. M. Sidi Mohammed left the Bardo under a salute from the guns, one of the wads of which nearly hit Captain Balfour on the head.

s: Sidi Mohammed does not smoke tobacco (described as extraordinary in Tunis)
q: The Bey did not smoke--a thing extraordinary, as nearly all men smoke in Tunis.

s: Sidi Mohammed dines alone (during the expeditions)
q: His Highness always dined alone.

s: Kairwan is a city
q: Few Christians arrive in this city.

s: house of the Kaed is a dwelling (good specimen of dwellings in the country)
q: The house of the Kaed was a good specimen of dwellings in this country.

s: Si Smyle teaches R. (Arabic during the tour)
q: Si Smyle (a very intelligent and learned man, and who taught Mr. R. Arabic during the tour)

s: Sidi Amour Abeda is a Moorish saint (regarded as a man of exceeding sanctity)
q: they said he was Sidi Amour Abeda, a man of exceeding sanctity

s: Sidi Amour Abeda has revered hands hands kissed by those who meet him (with devout and slavering obeisance)
q: Sidi Amour Abeda's hands ought to be lily-white, for every one who meets him kisses them with devout and slavering obeisance.

s: Sidi Amour Abeda has burial house little house (built by order of the Bey for his future remains)
q: We afterwards saw a little house, in course of erection by order of the Bey, where the remains of Sidi Amour Abeda are to be deposited at his death

s: Moorish saints require lineal descent descendant of the Prophet (essential ingredient in sainthood)
q: In this city, a lineal descendant of the Prophet, and a lucky guesser in the way of divining, are the essential ingredients in the composition of a Moorish saint.

s: Moorish saints require divining ability lucky guesser (essential ingredient in sainthood)
q: In this city, a lineal descendant of the Prophet, and a lucky guesser in the way of divining, are the essential ingredients in the composition of a Moorish saint.

s: Moorish saints are common in Kairwan (as thick as ordinary priests in Malta)
q: Saints of one order or another are as thick here as ordinary priests in Malta

s: renegade doctor of the Bey describes Sidi Amour Abeda (as wishing English infidels burnt alive)
q: The renegade doctor of the Bey told us that the old dervish now in question would like nothing better than to see us English infidels burnt alive.

s: Kairwan has cleanliness clean
q: The town is clean, but many houses are in ruins.

s: Bey of Tunis administers the administration of justice (morning and evening while at Kairwan)
q: We went to see his Highness administer justice, which he always did, morning and evening, whilst at Kairwan.

s: the administration of justice refers cases to kadys (some plaintiffs were referred for redress)
q: others were referred to the kadys and chiefs.

s: the administration of justice refers cases to chiefs (some plaintiffs were referred for redress)
q: others were referred to the kadys and chiefs.

s: Bey of Tunis owns camels (an immense number)
q: The Bey of Tunis has an immense number of camels which he farms out.

s: Bey's camel-farming system leases camels (for mills and agricultural labours at so much per head)
q: these let them out to other persons for mills and agricultural labours, at so much per head.

s: Bey's camel-farming system requires annual accounting camels (overseers render accounts to Government)
q: The overseers annually render an account of them to Government, and, when called upon, supply the number required.

s: Kairwan has ruined houses many
q: The town is clean, but many houses are in ruins.

s: Bey's camel seizure makes property of camels (animals seized for the Bey and marked 'taba')
q: which were then marked ("taba,") _a la Bey_, and immediately became the Bey's property.

s: Bey's camel seizure affects camels (about two hundred changed hands)
q: About two hundred changed hands in this way.

s: Bey of Tunis receives camels as compensation camels (thirty-three for tribal manslaughter)
q: If an Arab commits manslaughter, his tribe is mulcted thirty-three camels; and, as the crime is rather common in the Bedouin districts, the Bey's acquisition in this way is considerable.

s: Bey of Tunis remits duty for Sicilian nobleman (for about eighty camels exported to Sicily)
q: A few years ago, a Sicilian nobleman exported from Tunis to Sicily some eighty camels, the duty for which the Bey remitted.

s: camels is useful for vast plains (in North Africa, Arabia, Persia, Australasia, and some parts of the East Indies)
q: The camel is only useful where there are vast plains to travel, as in North Africa, Arabia, Persia, Australasia, and some parts of the East Indies.

s: camels cannot supersede mules (in the islands of the Mediterranean)
q: The camel, if ever so healthy and thriving in the islands of the Mediterranean, could never supersede the labour of mules.

s: Arabs are inspected by Bey of Tunis (in a single-file contingent)
q: A hundred more Arabs joined, who passed in a single file before the Bey for inspection

s: gazelles are faster than greyhound (making them difficult to catch)
q: but they go much faster than the greyhound

s: R. receives protection from Bey of Tunis (the Bey ordered punishment for an Arab who insulted him)
q: R. noticed the fellow, and afterwards told the Bey, who instantly ordered him to receive two hundred bastinadoes, and to be put in chains

s: Kairwan has quartered troops regiment of the Nitham (greater part quartered in the city)
q: The greater part of a regiment of the Nitham are quartered here.

s: Bey of Tunis uses bastinado punishment (ordered two hundred strokes and chains for an insult to R.)
q: who instantly ordered him to receive two hundred bastinadoes, and to be put in chains

s: Bey of Tunis presents black horse (to Captain B.)
q: The Bey surprised Captain B. by sending him a handsome black horse as a present

s: Bey of Tunis presents grey horse (to the Frenchman; replaced after complaint)
q: he also sent a grey one to the Frenchman, who, when complaining of it, saying that it was a bad one, to the Bey's mamelukes, his Highness sent for it, and gave him another.

s: Bey's ministers and mamelukes stops R. (for fear he might be insulted)
q: The old Governor was a great fanatic, and when R. ran up to shake hands with him, the mamelukes stopped R. for fear he might be insulted.

s: falcons carry off hares (part of a large hawking establishment)
q: We had a large hawking-establishment with us, some twenty birds, very fine falconry, which sometimes carried off hares, and even attacked young goat-kids.

s: Christians arrive in Kairwan (few)
q: Few Christians arrive in this city.

s: famous mosque (Kairwan) contains spoils from Christian churches (marble pillars and other ornaments)
q: The famous mosque, of course, we were not allowed to enter, but many of its marble pillars and other ornaments, we heard from Giovanni, were the spoils of Christian churches and Pagan temples.

s: famous mosque (Kairwan) contains spoils from Pagan temples (marble pillars and other ornaments)
q: The famous mosque, of course, we were not allowed to enter, but many of its marble pillars and other ornaments, we heard from Giovanni, were the spoils of Christian churches and Pagan temples.

s: gazelles is smaller than ebba (a little)
q: We came upon a herd of small deer, called ebba, which are a little larger than the gazelle

s: the expedition and camp includes camels (about two thousand)
q: We had two thousand camels with the camp and following it

s: camels subsist on coarse grass, weeds or thorns (no provender is carried for them)
q: for which not a single atom of provender is carried, the camels subsisting scantily upon the coarse grass, weeds or thorns, which the soil barely affords.

s: camels is called the ship of the Desert
q: This rude contrivance makes the camel more than ever "the ship of the Desert."

s: Ghafsa is a town (surrounded by olive and date trees)
q: A ride over sand-hills brought us in view of the town, embedded in olive and date-trees

s: Ghafsa has springs hot springs of Ghafsa (principally hot and mineral waters)
q: Ghafsa, [37] which is almost a mass of rubbish filled with dirty people, although there are plenty of springs about, principally hot and mineral waters.

s: hot springs of Ghafsa contain fish of the hot springs (the fish live in hot water)
q: In these Thermae, or hot, sulphurous, and other mineral springs, is the phenomenon of the existence of fish and small snakes.

s: hot springs of Ghafsa contain snake of the hot springs (the snake feeds entirely on fish)
q: The snake, not noticed by former tourists, has been observed by Mr. Honneger, which nourishes itself entirely upon the fish.

s: hot springs of Ghafsa have temperature ninety-five degrees (according to Sir Grenville Temple's observation)
q: Sir Grenville Temple remarks: "The thermometer in the water marked ninety-five degrees

s: Ghafsa has structure the Kasbah at Ghafsa (nearly ruined and built chiefly from ancient remains)
q: We inspected the old Kasbah at Ghafsa, which is in nearly a state of ruin, and looked as if it would soon be down about our ears. It is an irregular square, and built chiefly of the remains of ancient edifices.

s: Moors are enjoined to use baths (by their religion)
q: Although the Moors, by their religion, are enjoined the constant use of the bath

s: Arabs slaughter game with religious invocation (when securing an animal)
q: As soon as an Arab secures an animal, he immediately cuts its throat, repeating "Bismillah, Allah Akbar," "In the name (of God), God is great."

s: North Africa has salt and nitre efflorescence (across numerous plains)
q: Numerous plains in North Africa are covered with saline and nitrous efflorescence

s: Jereed has date palms (surrounding its towns)
q: Here was the village of Dra-el-Hammah, surrounded, like all the towns of the Jereed, with date-groves and gardens.

s: the Desert has water resources springs (described as bountiful but neglected by people)
q: God is bountiful in the Desert, but man wilfully neglects these aqueous riches springing up eternally to repair the ravages of the burning simoum!

s: water management in the desert could support ten thousand palms and forests of olives (through irrigation of the adjoining plain)
q: Water is so abundant, that the adjoining plain might be easily irrigated, and planted with ten thousand palms and forests of olives.

s: water management in the desert is controlled by Bey of Tunis (through orders sent to district Arabs)
q: when the camp arrives at Kairwan, the Bey sends an order to the Arabs of the district to let the water run down to the place where the tents are pitched.

s: Bey of Tunis has authority over Arabs (in managing water for the camp)
q: the Bey sends an order to the Arabs of the district to let the water run down to the place where the tents are pitched.

s: Toser is a town (in the Jereed)
q: Toser, or Touzer, the _Tisurus_ of ancient geography, is a considerable town of about six thousand souls, with several villages in its neighbourhood.

s: Toser's water system waters the gardens (divides itself afterwards in three branches)
q: running along the walls of the city southward, divides itself afterwards in three branches, waters the gardens, and, after having irrigated the plantations of several other villages, loses itself in the sand at a short distance

s: date cultivation and trade at Toser is almost only food dates (here)
q: The dates are almost the only food here, and the streets are literally gravelled with their stones.

s: date cultivation and trade at Toser is taxed by Bey of the Camp (at two bunches per date-tree)
q: The tax imposed is equivalent to two bunches for each date-tree.

s: Bey of the Camp administers justice Toser (morning and evening while in the Jereed)
q: The Bey administers justice, morning and evening, whilst in the Jereed.

s: Bey of the Camp has officers Bey's officers
q: A new Sheikh was installed, a good thing for the Bey's officers, as many of them got presents on the occasion.

s: Bey of the Camp has ministers and mamelukes Bey's ministers and mamelukes
q: The Bey and his ministers and mamelukes amused themselves with shooting at a mark.

s: Sheikh Tahid is a sheikh (the leading man at Toser)
q: The great man here is the Sheikh Tahid, who was imprisoned for not having the tribute ready for the Bey.

s: Sheikh Tahid collects tribute of the Jereed (for the Bey)
q: The Sheikh has to collect them, paying a certain yearly sum when the Bey arrives, a species of farming-out.

s: Sheikh Tahid is imprisoned by Bey of the Camp (for failing to have the tribute ready)
q: The great man here is the Sheikh Tahid, who was imprisoned for not having the tribute ready for the Bey.

s: Toser is a a considerable town (of about six thousand souls)
q: Toser, or Touzer, the _Tisurus_ of ancient geography, is a considerable town of about six thousand souls, with several villages in its neighbourhood.

s: tribute of the Jereed is assessed as two bunches for each date-tree
q: The tax imposed is equivalent to two bunches for each date-tree.

s: Santa Maria returned his horse (to the Bey)
q: Santa Maria again returned his horse to the Bey, and got another in its stead.

s: Santa Maria leaves for Ghabs (with an escort of twelve men)
q: Santa Maria left for Ghabs, to which place there is not a correct route laid down in any chart.

s: Jereed contains Toser (Toser is its headquarters)
q: we arrived at the top of a rising ground, at the base of which was situate the famous Toser, the head-quarters of the camp in the Jereed

s: Nefta is a frontier town (of the Tunisian territories to the south)
q: is the frontier town of the Tunisian territories from the south, being five days' journey, or about thirty-five or forty leagues from the oases of Souf, and fifteen days' from Ghadumes

s: Nefta is called the gate of Tunis (by the Arabs)
q: Nefta is the intermediate _entrepot_ of commerce which Tunis pours towards the Sahara, and for this reason is called by the Arabs, "the gate of Tunis;"

s: Nefta is governed by Nefta's Shereefs (the Bey usually chooses governors from among them)
q: The Shereefs are the genuine nobles, or seigneurs of Nefta, from among whom the Bey is wont to choose the Governors of the city.

s: Nefta is an intermediate entrepot for commerce which Tunis pours towards the Sahara
q: Nefta is the intermediate _entrepot_ of commerce which Tunis pours towards the Sahara

s: Toser has population about six thousand souls
q: Toser, or Touzer, the _Tisurus_ of ancient geography, is a considerable town of about six thousand souls, with several villages in its neighbourhood.

s: Tunis sends commerce through Nefta (towards the Sahara)
q: Nefta is the intermediate _entrepot_ of commerce which Tunis pours towards the Sahara

s: Sahara mirage resembles water (the salt surface appears to be a sea)
q: On our return from Toser, we had an extensive view of the Sahara, an ocean as far as the eye could see, of what one would have taken his oath was water

s: Sahara mirage is caused by salt scattered on the surface
q: but, in reality, nothing but salt scattered on the surface.

s: Toser has gardens date-trees (beautiful and abundantly watered)
q: The gardens, however, under the date-trees are beautiful, and abundantly watered with copious streams, all of which are warm, and in one of which we bathed ourselves and felt new vigour run through our veins.

s: Toser contains mosques, schools, Moorish baths, and fondouks
q: Toser has mosques, schools, Moorish baths--a luxury rare on the confines of the Desert, fondouks or inns, &c.

s: Toser produces dates (of the finest quality)
q: The dates of Toser are esteemed of the finest quality.

s: Toser produces burnouses (through household industry)
q: They make many burnouses at Toser, and every house presents the industrious sight of the needle or shuttle quickly moving.

s: Toser has water supply Wad Meshra (the city’s wells are insufficient)
q: The wells within the city of Toser are insufficient for the consumption of the inhabitants, who fetch water from Wad Meshra.

s: sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens is a sale
q: The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres

s: Captain B. prefers Trungah (among the date varieties)
q: Captain B. preferred the Trungah, another first-rate sort, which are plum-shaped, and taste something like a plum.

s: dates are fine very fine (not abundant)
q: The dates were very fine, though in no very great abundance

s: Jereed has rainfall rainfall in the Jereed (a single day during the past year)
q: the superior state of ripeness being attributed to there only being a single day of rain during the past year in the Jereed.

s: dates are harmed by rain (rain is bad for the dates)
q: Rain is bad for the dates, but the roots of the tree cannot have too much water.

s: date harvest has ripeness superior (attributed to limited rainfall in the Jereed)
q: the superior state of ripeness being attributed to there only being a single day of rain during the past year in the Jereed.

s: Moorish feastdays include lascivious actions (performed by men and women as indispensable entertainment)
q: But, on all Moorish feastdays, lascivious actions of men and women are an indispensable part of their entertainment.

s: sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens price 15,000 piastres
q: The Sheikh Tahib's gardens were sold for 15,000 piastres

s: Moors have character lascivious (described as their worst side)
q: This is the worst side of the character of the Moors.

s: Sultan Kaed is a chief (of the Hammama)
q: One of the greatest chiefs, Sultan Kaed, of the Hammama has just died.

s: Sultan Kaed belongs to Hammama (chief)
q: One of the greatest chiefs, Sultan Kaed, of the Hammama has just died.

s: Sultan Kaed has age extremely old (at death)
q: He was an extremely old man

s: death of Sultan Kaed is a death
q: One of the greatest chiefs, Sultan Kaed, of the Hammama has just died.

s: Sultan Kaed distinguishes himself in French conflict before Constantina (during his life; lastly before Constantina)
q: During his life, he had often distinguished himself, and lastly against the French, before Constantina.

s: Arab encounter in the hills involves Arabs (about nine Arabs encountered in the hills)
q: Whilst in the hills one day, we came suddenly upon a set of Arabs, about nine in number

s: Sheikh Tahib's wife contributes to sale of Sheikh Tahib's gardens (additional contribution)
q: his wife also added to this 1,000

s: loted is a deer-like animal (about the size of a fallow deer)
q: The head of the loted is like a deer's, but the eye is further up: it is about a fallowdeer's size.

s: loted has head deer-like head (the eye is positioned farther up)
q: The head of the loted is like a deer's, but the eye is further up

s: loted has sexual dimorphism female lacks a beard (unlike a goat)
q: The female has not the beard like a goat

s: loted has hair long hair (on the female, from head to bottom of chest and over the fore-legs)
q: but long hair, reaching from the head to the bottom of the chest, and over the fore-legs.

s: Sheikh Ali hunts loted (shot a female and its young one)
q: The Sheikh Ali brought in two loteds, a female and its young one, which he had shot.

s: Bey's order to bring in loteds issued by Bey of the Camp
q: in consequence of an order from the Bey

s: dates are harvested date harvest (in considerable quantity)
q: The dates have been coming in to a great amount.

s: date harvest contains Degalah (most esteemed variety)
